Terra Through Time · vol. 1

A world made of columns

Sixty-four thousand eight hundred columns, one for every degree of latitude and longitude, standing in for the surface of the earth. Switch what they're showing and the whole field reads itself again.

What the six views mean

Elevation raises the land into real terrain and sinks the sea floor into real basins, colored the way a printed relief map is. Relief measures how sharply the ground changes rather than how high it sits, so mountain chains, coastlines and the mid-ocean ridges stand out while plains and abyssal basins stay flat. Tides turns the sea into water, breathing in and out on a stylized day cycle; the land holds still.

Three more views read the same grid through two centuries of people. Population turns height into headcount: drag the year, or press play, and watch the map fill in from the empires and colonies of 1800, through the industrial cities of 1900 and the postwar surge, to the world as it stands today. Density divides that by how much ground a cell actually covers, since a one-degree cell near the poles is a fraction of the size of one at the equator. Growth shows the change since the previous decade rather than the total, which is where the demographic transition becomes visible as it moves across the world.

Hovering

Point at any land cell and the map names the country, shows its flag, and gives its population for the year currently selected, along with what that was a decade earlier and the country's share of the world at that moment. The numbers are per country, not per cell: this grid is too coarse to say anything honest about a single square degree.

How it moves

All sixty-four thousand columns are drawn in a single instanced call, with height and color resolved on the GPU, so nothing depends on JavaScript touching each column every frame. Moving between two years interpolates between the two decades on either side of it, and moving between two datasets cross-fades every column on a staggered delay, which is what makes the change read as a wave rather than a switch.

Sources
Population, and the per-country figures on hover: Our World in Data's long-run population series (Gapminder, HYDE and the UN), sampled at each keyframe decade from 1800 to 2023.

Country boundaries: Natural Earth 1:110m, rasterised to this one-degree grid. At this resolution a country smaller than roughly one degree across may not occupy a cell of its own, and coastal cells are assigned to the nearest land neighbour.

Land relief: a NASA-derived global elevation raster, sampled to the same grid. It is relative relief, not metres, which is why no elevation figure is quoted on hover.

Sea floor: derived from the bathymetric tint of the original relief image and rank-normalised, so ordering by depth is real while the absolute scale is not.

Density and Growth are derived here rather than measured separately: density by dividing population by the cosine-of-latitude area of each cell, growth by differencing consecutive decades. Country population is spread evenly across that country's land cells, so Density compares countries rather than cities; it is not a true population-density map.
